questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify which listed item enters gross domestic product
questions.stem: A statistician lists four candidate items for one country's output in a single calendar year. Which one belongs in that country's gross domestic product for the year?

options.text: Bread baked inside the country and sold to households there during the year
Flour the same bakery buys from a mill in order to bake that bread during the year
options.misconception: counts an intermediate good that is already embedded in the final product

options.text: Bread a household bakes at home from flour it bought in a shop
options.misconception: treats unmeasured household production as though it entered the accounts

options.text: A car built inside the country in an earlier year and resold here this year
options.misconception: counts the resale of an old good as production inside the period

questions.explanation: Gross domestic product counts final goods and services produced inside the borders during the period measured, so the bread baked and sold locally qualifies. The flour fails because it is an intermediate good whose value is already inside the bread, and adding both would record the same production twice. Home baking is real production but is not measured, so the accounts miss it rather than wrongly include it, and reselling a car built last year is a transfer of an existing asset with no current production behind it.
questions.hint: Test each item against finality, domestic location, and the period.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why intermediate goods are left out of output
questions.stem: In one year a mill sells flour to a bakery for 600, and the bakery sells bread to households for 1,000. Why does the national accounts record 1,000 of output rather than 1,600?

options.text: Because adding the flour as well would record the same production twice over
Because the mill's output is valued at its costs of production rather than at its price
options.misconception: believes intermediate output is measured by its costs rather than by its selling price

options.text: Because only what households pay counts, so all business payments are left out
options.misconception: believes only household spending is recorded, ignoring business purchases

options.text: Because intermediate goods may only ever be counted as investment in equipment
options.misconception: believes an intermediate good can only be capital formation and never output

questions.explanation: The 600 of flour is not additional production; it is the same physical material, carried forward into the bread, and the bread's 1,000 already contains it. Summing both stages gives 1,600 and counts the flour twice. Intermediate goods are not valued at cost because there is no rule that treats them that way, they are excluded precisely because their value reappears in the price of the final good, and nothing about the flour restricts it to being counted as investment.
questions.hint: Ask how many times the value of the flour appears in the 1,000.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute output by summing value added at each stage
questions.stem: In one week a farm sells wheat for 600 to a mill, the mill sells flour for 1,000 to a bakery, the bakery sells bread for 1,500 to a shop, and the shop sells that bread for 1,900 to households. All four stages are inside the country, all amounts are currency per week, and each sale is final for its own stage. What is that week's gross domestic product in currency?
questions.explanation: Value added at each stage is that stage's output minus the intermediate inputs it bought: the farm adds 600 with no intermediate inputs, the mill adds 1,000 minus 600 equals 400, the bakery adds 1,500 minus 1,000 equals 500, and the shop adds 1,900 minus 1,500 equals 400. The total is 600 + 400 + 500 + 400 = 1,900 currency per week, which equals the price of the only final good, confirming the figure by a second route. Adding the four stage sales instead gives 600 + 1,000 + 1,500 + 1,900 = 5,000, overstating output because the 600, 1,000, and 1,500 are each counted again inside the next stage's price. The assumption is that every stage is domestic and that nothing is produced for own use.
questions.hint: Subtract each stage's purchases of inputs from that stage's own sales.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Value added and the final good
questions.learningObjective: explain why summing value added equals the value of final output
questions.stem: Two approaches measure a year's output: adding the market value of every final good and service produced, or adding what each producing industry contributes beyond the inputs it bought. Why do the two totals agree?

options.text: Each stage's value added equals its own selling price minus the intermediate inputs it bought
Both approaches ignore prices entirely, since only physical volumes of output are counted
options.misconception: believes national accounts count quantities rather than the values of output

options.text: The industry approach gives the larger total, because it captures every intermediate sale
options.misconception: believes adding value across stages necessarily counts some output twice

options.text: The totals match only in countries that import and export nothing during the period
options.misconception: believes open trade is what breaks the equivalence between the two totals

questions.explanation: Along any chain of production, each stage's value added is its output price minus the price it paid for inputs from earlier stages, and those earlier prices are exactly the items deducted further down the chain. Every subtraction therefore cancels one prior sale and leaves the final price, so summing value added and summing final goods arrive at the same figure. Neither approach ignores prices, since the totals are measured in currency, summing value added cannot include an intermediate sale twice because each was netted out, and the cancellation works identically whether or not a country trades.
questions.hint: Follow one chain of production and see what each subtraction cancels.

questions.learningObjective: decide which part of a resale is current production
questions.stem: A household sells a ten-year-old car to a neighbour for 2,000, and the dealer who arranged the sale charges a 200 brokerage fee. Which statement about this year's measured output is correct?

options.misconception: believes any money changing hands in a sale is current production

options.misconception: believes a market transaction on its own makes a good count as output

options.text: The 2,000 is recorded as consumption and the 200 fee is excluded as a pure service
options.misconception: believes brokerage services fall outside the production boundary

The brokerage fee, by contrast, pays for a service performed now, so the 200 is current output. Transactions do not by themselves create production, and a brokerage arrangement service is plainly inside the production boundary, which is why the fee is the whole of this year's addition.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute output from the four expenditure components
questions.stem: A country's national accounts for one year, in billions of currency, report consumption 2,400, gross private investment 800, government purchases 1,100, exports 700, and imports 900. Net factor income from abroad is zero and there is no depreciation. What is that country's gross domestic product for the year, in billions of currency?
questions.explanation: The expenditure identity is GDP = C + I + G + (X - M), so 2,400 + 800 + 1,100 + (700 - 900) = 4,300 plus net exports of minus 200, giving 4,100 billion currency. Net exports are negative because the 900 of imports exceeds the 700 of exports, and that excess is deducted rather than added. The same figure follows a second route by adding the four positive flows and then removing imports: 2,400 + 800 + 1,100 + 700 = 5,000, less 900, equals 4,100. The assumptions are that all five figures are current-price measures for the same year and that inventories are already inside gross investment.
questions.hint: Net exports subtracts imports, and imports here exceed exports.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: decide which payments count as investment in output
questions.stem: A firm spends 500 on machinery, builds 300 of finished goods that remain unsold at year end, and pays 200 for a stake in another firm's shares. Which of that spending is investment in the national accounts?

options.text: The 500 of machinery and the 300 of unsold output, but not the share purchase
The 500 of machinery alone, because goods not yet sold are not yet part of output
options.misconception: believes only goods already sold can count as investment

options.text: The 200 paid for shares alone, because buying equity funds future production
options.misconception: believes buying a financial claim is the same as buying a capital good

options.text: All 1,000 of it, because any payment that reaches a firm is capital formation
options.misconception: believes every business-to-business payment counts as investment

questions.explanation: Investment in the accounts is the addition to produced capital, so the 500 of machinery qualifies and the 300 of unsold finished goods qualifies as an addition to inventories, which is investment precisely because it has not yet been consumed. The 200 for a share is a purchase of a claim on an existing asset, so it swaps one owner's financial asset for another's without creating new capital. Only goods already sold are counted as final sales on the consumption side, which is why unsold output is capital formation rather than consumption, and the test is whether a produced asset has grown, not simply whether a firm was paid.
questions.hint: Ask whether the payment adds to produced capital or only moves a claim.

questions.stem: In one year a government pays 400 in unemployment benefits and 300 in interest on its own outstanding debt. Which part of that spending appears in the government's contribution to measured output?

Only the 300, because paying interest is a cost of producing government services
options.misconception: believes interest payments buy current government output

options.text: Only the 400, since benefits are a transfer while interest is a purchase
options.misconception: believes transfer payments count and interest payments do not

options.text: Both figures, since every payment out of the public purse is a final purchase
options.misconception: believes all government outlays are final purchases of output

Interest is a return on past borrowing rather than the cost of producing this year's government services, so it fails the test just as the benefit does.

questions.stem: In one year a country exports 900 of goods and services and imports 1,200. What does that imply about its net exports, and about what foreign trade does to its measured output?

Net exports are positive 300, so the excess of exports adds to domestic output
options.misconception: reverses the sign by treating the export flow as the larger one

options.text: Net exports are negative 300, but foreign trade always adds to domestic output
options.misconception: believes net exports can never reduce a country's measured output

options.text: Net exports are zero, because goods and services cancel once trade is counted
options.misconception: believes exports and imports always offset each other exactly

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state what distinguishes nominal from real output
questions.stem: One country's output total is valued at the prices prevailing in the year itself, and another's is valued at the prices of a fixed base year. What practical difference does that make between the two figures?

options.text: The first rises when prices rise even with output unchanged; the second strips that out
The first counts only goods, while the second also counts services in every period
options.misconception: believes the two measures differ in which outputs they cover

options.text: The first uses a base year, while the second uses the prices of the current year
options.misconception: swaps which measure uses current prices and which uses base prices

options.text: The two always grow at the same rate whenever real output is rising at all
options.misconception: believes current and base price measures move in lockstep

questions.explanation: Valuing output at current prices means a price rise alone lifts the total even if the same goods are produced, so the nominal series mixes quantity and price movements. Valuing the same output at fixed base year prices strips the price movement out, leaving only the change in the quantity of goods and services. The two measures cover an identical set of outputs in both cases, it is the current-price measure that embeds this year's prices while the base-year measure freezes them, and the two series can certainly diverge in any year when prices and output move in different directions.

questions.learningObjective: interpret what a deflator value measures
questions.stem: A gross domestic product deflator of 118 is reported for a year in which the base year carries an index of 100. What does that single published number tell you about prices?

options.text: The average price of all goods and services, imported ones included, rose 18 percent
options.misconception: believes the deflator's coverage includes imported goods and services

options.text: Every individual price in the economy rose by exactly 18 percent that year
options.misconception: believes one price index describes every individual price in the economy

A fixed consumer basket is the construction used by a consumer price index, not by the deflator, and the deflator's numerator covers domestic production only, so imported goods are outside it. Because it is a ratio of two totals it describes an average, so individual prices may move by very different amounts in either direction.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: convert a two year price level change into an annual rate
questions.stem: A country's gross domestic product deflator stands at 100 in one year and at 121.5 two years later, with the earlier year as the base. What is the average annual rate of price change over those two years, in percent to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: The price level rose 21.5 percent in total, so an average annual rate r must satisfy (1 + r)^2 = 1.215, giving r = 1.215^0.5 - 1 = 1.102270 - 1 = 0.10227, or 10.23 percent a year. Back-substitution confirms the figure by a second route: 1.10227 x 1.10227 = 1.215000, exactly the ratio of the two index readings. The tempting shortcut of halving 21.5 to get 10.75 is only an approximation, and it overstates the true rate because compounding makes each year's increase work on a larger base than the first.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the two year price ratio, not half the cumulative change.

questions.topic: Limits of real growth as a welfare measure
questions.learningObjective: identify what a real growth rate leaves out
questions.stem: A country's real gross domestic product rises 3 percent in a year, yet survey respondents report no improvement in their own circumstances. What must the real growth figure be failing to capture?

options.text: Whether the extra output reached people widely or went mostly to a few
Whether the increase was measured at current prices or at base year prices
options.misconception: believes a real growth rate is ambiguous about its price basis

options.text: Whether the economy produced goods or services during the reported year
options.misconception: believes a real growth figure says nothing about goods against services

options.text: Whether the counting period was a calendar year or a full twelve months
options.misconception: believes a growth rate conceals how long the period measured was

A real figure is by construction already valued at fixed base year prices, so the price basis is settled rather than open, and it does cover both goods and services because the accounts measure both. The period is stated whenever a growth rate is published, so the one thing the total genuinely cannot tell you is who received the extra output.

questions.learningObjective: explain why the income approach equals the expenditure approach
questions.stem: One agency measures a year's output by adding up the final spending on it. Another adds up the incomes earned in producing it, namely wages, rent, interest, and profit. Why must the two totals agree?

questions.learningObjective: state how national income differs from gross domestic product
questions.stem: Gross domestic product is measured at market prices, while national income is struck after removing the capital consumed in production and after removing indirect taxes. What follows for the relationship between the two?

The two measures are always identical, since both count the same final goods once
options.misconception: believes depreciation and indirect taxes cancel out in the national accounts

options.text: National income is the larger measure, because it adds every tax back into income

options.text: They differ only by the country's net factor income from abroad in each period

questions.learningObjective: identify disposable personal income and how it is obtained
questions.stem: Which measure represents the income households actually have available to spend or save, and how is that measure obtained from personal income?

options.text: Disposable personal income, which is personal income less personal taxes
National income, which is output less depreciation and less indirect taxes
options.misconception: names the aggregate income measure rather than the disposable one

options.text: Gross domestic product, which is final output valued at prices prevailing in the year
options.misconception: stops at the market value stage without removing personal taxes

options.text: Gross national product, which adds net factor income earned from abroad
options.misconception: adjusts for foreign factor income but leaves personal taxes in

options.text: A's national product is 1,120 and B's is 920, because ownership of assets differs
Both have national product of 1,000, because the measure ignores who owns assets
options.misconception: believes national product ignores cross-border ownership

options.text: A's is 1,120 and B's is 1,080, because an outflow abroad is added rather than subtracted
options.misconception: adds a negative net item instead of subtracting it

options.text: A's is 880 and B's is 1,080, because the adjustment runs in the opposite direction
options.misconception: reverses the sign of the net factor income adjustment

questions.explanation: Adding net factor income from abroad to domestic output gives A 1,000 + 120 = 1,120 and B 1,000 + (-80) = 920 billion currency, so the same domestic total supports a different national product depending on who owns the factors at home. A 1,080 for B would result from adding the absolute value of an outflow, which is the opposite of what the net figure means.

questions.topic: Per person figures when population outruns output
questions.learningObjective: interpret per person output when population grows faster
questions.stem: A country's real gross domestic product grows by 2.5 percent over a year, and its population grows by 4.0 percent. Which statement about real output per person is correct?

options.text: It falls by about 1.4 percent, because population grew faster than real output
It rises by about 1.5 percent, because real output grew at all
options.misconception: infers a per person rise from any rise in the total

options.text: It is unchanged, because a per person figure cannot depend on population
options.misconception: believes a per person measure is independent of the population

options.text: It falls by exactly 1.5 percent, because 2.5 minus 4 is the exact change
options.misconception: subtracts the rates and calls the difference exact

questions.explanation: The per person factor is the output growth factor over the population growth factor, so 1.025 / 1.04 - 1 = -0.014423, a fall of about 1.4 percent. The adjusted-difference route agrees: (0.025 - 0.04) / 1.04 = -0.014423, the same figure. A per person measure divides by population by construction, so it cannot be independent of it, and a rise in the total is no guarantee of a rise per person when the denominator grows faster than the numerator. Subtracting the rates to get exactly -1.5 percent is the linear approximation and ignores the compounding.
questions.hint: Divide the two growth factors and keep the sign.

questions.stem: Apply the identity that value added equals output minus intermediate inputs to one stage of a chain. What is the processor's value added per month?

1,250, being the processor's own selling price for the month

options.text: 2,050, being the grower's 800 added to the processor's 1,250
options.misconception: sums the stage outputs and double counts the input

options.misconception: computes the retailer's value added instead

560, being 800 divided by the price factor instead of multiplied
options.misconception: divides by the price factor when rebuilding a nominal figure

options.text: 80, being 1.40 taken off 800 as a percentage deduction
options.misconception: treats the deflator as a rate to be subtracted

The division by 100 is what turns the index into a factor, and once that is done the real figure must be multiplied, because a deflator above 100 means the same output costs more than it did in the base year. Dividing would understate the nominal figure, and a deflator is a multiplier rather than a rate to be deducted.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain the double counting an intermediate good would cause
questions.stem: Explain why adding the value of an intermediate good to the value of the final good that contains it would overstate the output of a period.

answer.exemplar: The value of the intermediate good is already contained in the price of the final good, because the firm that buys the input pays for it and passes that cost into what it charges. Take wheat at 600 sold to a mill, flour at 1,000 sold to a bakery, and bread at 1,500 sold to a shop. The 600 of wheat and the 1,000 of flour are both present inside the 1,500, so recording the 1,500 and then adding 1,000 and 600 records the same physical value three times over. The output of the period is the value newly created, which is the sum of the value added at each stage, 600 + 400 + 500 = 1,500. The accounting works because every intermediate sale is matched by an equal purchase that the next stage subtracts, so the double count cancels exactly.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to trace one chain of sales and show the input's value reappearing inside the downstream price, because a bare statement that counting both would double count does not show why. The matching purchase and subtraction is what makes the correction exact rather than approximate.
questions.hint: Follow one chain of sales and look for the input's value inside the next price.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: What a deflator's base year does
questions.learningObjective: explain how the base year choice affects a deflator reading
questions.stem: Explain how the choice of base year changes what a gross domestic product deflator reports, and what it leaves unchanged.

answer.exemplar: The base year fixes the year whose price level is set equal to 100, so every deflator reading is a statement about prices relative to that year rather than an absolute level. With a deflator of 100 in the base year and 110 in the next, the newer prices are 10 percent above the base year's. Move the base forward one year and the rescaling 100 x (100 / 110) puts the earlier year at about 90.9, so the index level moves while the ratio between the two years, and therefore the 10 percent price rise between them, is untouched. What changes is the reference point, and with it every reading's distance from 100; what does not change is the measured inflation between any two years, which is why rebased series can be compared over the same pair of dates.

questions.explanation: A model answer must separate the index level, which is arbitrary, from the ratio between years, which is not, because the whole of the point is that rebasing rescales without distorting the measured price change.
questions.hint: Separate what the rescaling changes from what it leaves fixed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Why real growth is the better production measure
questions.learningObjective: explain why real growth isolates changes in production
questions.stem: Explain why a growth rate measured in base year prices is a better index of changes in production than one measured at current prices.

answer.exemplar: A current price total moves with two things at once, the quantity of goods produced and the prices those goods fetch, so it cannot separate them. If prices rise 8 percent and the nominal total rises 5 percent, the quantity of output has fallen, because 1.05 divided by 1.08 leaves 0.9728 of the earlier level, a fall of 2.78 percent, even though the headline figure rose. Valuing the same output at fixed base year prices removes the price term from the ratio, leaving only the change in the quantity of goods and services, which is what a measure of production is supposed to report. The cost is that a single base year prices distant years at outdated relative prices, which is why no base year makes the measure exact for every comparison, but between nearby years the price term is the larger distortion and real growth is the better index.

questions.explanation: A model answer must show the price term being divided out with a worked case, since the claim is quantitative: the current price total conflates two movements and the deflated one does not.
questions.hint: Show what happens to the growth rate once the price change is divided out.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: The paradox of thrift in detail
questions.learningObjective: explain why intended saving need not become actual saving
questions.stem: Explain why an attempt by a nation's households to save more can leave the nation with no more saving than before.

answer.exemplar: Household saving is spending income that is not consumed, so when every household cuts its spending at once the spending someone else had planned on does not happen, and with prices and wages sticky the firms that lost those sales cut output and income instead of cutting their prices. National income therefore falls, and the intended saving is divided over a smaller income. If households try to save 100 extra in total but national income falls by 200, actual saving rises by only 100 of new income less the 200 of income lost, leaving it no higher than before, which is the paradox of thrift. The community has achieved neither the higher saving it wanted nor the higher investment that saving would have financed, because the contraction in spending cancels the increase in restraint. The paradox depends on prices not adjusting immediately: with fully flexible prices the lower spending would lower prices, raise real income, and partly restore both output and saving.

questions.explanation: A model answer must carry the arithmetic of intended saving against lost income, because the paradox is not that thrift is undesirable but that the private intention and the aggregate outcome diverge when prices are sticky.
questions.hint: Set the extra intended saving against the income lost from the spending cut.

6.0 percent, because the nominal total rose by that much

224,000, being the 2,800 of gross sector output divided by the population
options.misconception: divides gross sector output instead of value added

options.text: 40,000, being the 500 of farming value added scaled to the population
options.misconception: counts only one sector's value added

options.text: 128,000, being the 1,600 of cross sector inputs divided by the population
options.misconception: divides the intermediate purchases instead of the value added

questions.topic: From a propensity to a multiplier result
questions.learningObjective: build a multiplier from a propensity and apply it
questions.stem: A country's households spend 70 cents of each extra unit of income they receive, its tax rate is zero, and it imports nothing. The government raises purchases by 60 billion currency. First find the spending multiplier implied by that propensity, then apply it to the injection to find the change in output, in billions of currency.

options.text: 200, since the multiplier is 1 divided by 0.30 and 60 times 3.33 is 200
180, since the multiplier is 1 divided by the propensity to consume itself
options.misconception: divides by the propensity to consume rather than the propensity to save

options.text: 42, since 60 times 0.70 counts only the first round of respending
options.misconception: counts the first round of respending and stops

options.text: 600, since the multiplier is 1 divided by the 0.10 saved from each unit
options.misconception: divides by a saving rate that does not match the stated propensity

The second route adds up the rounds: 60 x (1 + 0.7 + 0.49 + further powers) = 60 / (1 - 0.7) = 60 / 0.3 = 200, the same figure. Counting only 60 x 0.7 = 42 stops after the first round and misses the whole point of the multiplier, and dividing by the propensity to consume rather than the propensity to save inverts the relationship between the multiplier and the two propensities.
questions.hint: Turn the spending propensity into a saving propensity, then invert it.

options.misconception: subtracts a positive net item instead of adding it

options.text: 1,720, because both cross border flows are added to domestic output
options.misconception: adds the outflow to income instead of netting it off

options.text: 1,400, because the two cross border flows always cancel within a year
options.misconception: assumes cross border factor income always nets to zero

questions.hint: Net the two cross border flows before applying them to domestic output.
